title: Classical guitar
summary: Gt-S1's plucked nylon treble strings on the body of the 1964 Esteso classical guitar, assembled from the plan Zimmer and Mores published in 2024: the braced spruce top with its sound hole, the barred rosewood back, the rosewood ribs, a rosewood bridge and the air inside, 20 shell parts on a 12 mm mesh. One string sounds at a time: G3, B3 and E4 open, F#4 and F5 stopped on the B string, each with 24 bending modes in two polarizations, plucked 120 mm from the saddle, the normal position in Traube's 2004 thesis. Each open string's tension was set by tuning the model's own fundamental to equal temperament; no recording sets a value. The body's air resonance is at 94 Hz and its first top-and-back resonance at 192 Hz, where 98 and 200 Hz were measured on this guitar. It is one 1964 Madrid guitar, not the Iowa recordings' Raimundo 118. The other five strings, wound bass strings and the player's finger are missing, and the pluck is one point at a station from the literature, not one measured on the recordings' player.
physics_present: Each string is a convergent modal beam with 24 bending modes in each of two transverse polarizations, with nylon density and bending modulus from Lynch-Aird and Woodhouse 2017 (harp-string proxy) and gauges from the D'Addario EJ45 specification

Tension is set per open string by the frozen setup protocol on this render's own fundamental (57.367, 58.446 and 78.822 N for G3, B3 and E4), never from a recording; D'Addario's chart values, 7.7 to 8.7 percent lower, are a cross-check only. F#4 and F5 are the B string stopped at the 7th and 18th frets, at its open-string tension

The string's bending modes above the 24 kept carry their exact static compliance into the saddle (residual flexibility): on E4 it softens the saddle spring from 100000 to about 25600 N/m and lowers the fundamentals by 7 to 8 cents, which the protocol's tensions restore

The string's second polarization, parallel to the top, reaches the body through the same 100000 N/m penalty spring at the top edge of the bridge wall, directly above the saddle point, with the same residual flexibility. The 45-degree pluck splits between the two polarizations, and the body's cross mobility couples them, so some partials decay in two stages
String loss: nylon viscoelastic bending loss from Woodhouse and Lynch-Aird 2019 (Kelvin-Voigt equivalent at 2 kHz), and air drag from the declared air as the renderer's per-mode resistance

The body of the 1964 Esteso guitar from Zimmer and Mores' 2024 plan (data/instruments/geometry/guitar-esteso-1964-zimmer2024), assembled by assemble-shell from its 12 mm shell table with the table generator's bridge: the top (2.47 mm, Sitka spruce) with its sound hole and 11 spruce braces, the back (2.31 mm, Rio rosewood) with four cedar bars, rosewood ribs (1.63 mm), and the bridge as a rosewood wall 182.8 x 28 mm, 8.7 mm high with the printed scooped ends; 20 parts, 5907 nodes and 22 ties. Body modes are kept from 15 Hz to 2 kHz

Wood constants from the Wood Handbook (FPL-GTR-282); wood loss from measurements on other samples: Qiu et al. 2026 for Sitka spruce with Bremaud, Gril and Thibaut's 2011 directional ratios, their padauk row standing in for Rio rosewood, and their softwood median standing in for cedar

The enclosed air with the 43.5 mm sound hole as a physical neck. In the body-mode solve of the same table (shell_body_modes) the open-hole air resonance is 93.9 Hz and the first top-and-back resonance 192.4 Hz, where Zimmer and Mores measured 98 and 200 Hz; the effective mass at the strings in the first top mode, sound hole sealed, is 77 to 147 g, where Wright 1996 measured 54 to 62 g on a classical guitar
Each string drives the top at its own point on the bridge line, at the inferred bridge station x = 334.54 mm, midway between the two axis strips
Pressure is the compact baffled, zero-retardation observation of the body and the sound hole at an assumed 1 m
F5 renders at 96 kHz: at 48 kHz its coupled stiffness fails the solver's stability screen
physics_missing: The other five strings: one string sounds at a time, so sympathetic strings are absent

The pluck: one point released 2 mm at 120 mm from the saddle on every note, the normal plucking position in Traube's 2004 thesis, not one measured on the recordings' player. On the open strings it places partials 4 and 8 where the recordings have them; the earlier 160 mm station, near a quarter of the string, silenced them. F5 is the B string stopped at the 18th fret, 230 mm long, so the same station is near its middle: partial 2 sits 36 dB below the fundamental and the even partials nearly vanish, where the recordings' F5 has them. A finger or nail about a centimetre wide is not modelled

The nylon's tension loss (eta_F) enters as zero: the tension-loss evidence table has no nylon row. Woodhouse 2017 accounts for measured nylon strings on a guitar with air, body and bending loss alone, and this render's partials already decay at least 1.3 times faster than that account. The recordings' partials decay faster still (E4 about twice), with their strings' brand and age and the Raimundo's body unknown
The unsteady-Stokes cylinder loading of the string by the air (its added mass and viscous memory) is not selected; air drag is the per-mode resistance only

Convergence: 24 bending modes per polarization end the partials at 4.7 kHz for G3 and 7.9 kHz for E4. From 12 to 24 modes the fundamental moved by -11.4, -11.2, -10.6 and -5.5 cents (G3, B3, E4, F#4, on the plate, without residual flexibility). The 12 mm body mesh and the 2 kHz body-mode window are not converged
The output is 16-bit PCM at a full scale of 1 Pa: band power above about 3 to 5 kHz is at the PCM16 quantisation floor, so the render cannot show or test any content there

The body is one 1964 Madrid guitar's plan, not the Iowa Raimundo 118. Each part has one thickness (the cube root of the mean cube of its printed points). The neck and heel, tail and heel blocks, linings, rosette, fingerboard, the patch under the bridge, the string holes, the central back strip and back patches, glue compliance and finish are left out

The bridge: the plan names no bridge wood (rosewood is assumed) and prints no bridge position (the station is inferred); the wall is thicker than it is tall, outside thin-shell validity, kept for its mass and beam stiffness
The string meets the body through an authored penalty spring (100000 N/m), not the saddle's contact mechanics
Wound bass strings: the multifilament core and the silver-plated winding dimensions are unknown
Finger and nail contact, the finger or fret contact of stopped notes (the fret is a rigid pinned end), and the player's holding contacts

The body's losses and its mass at the strings, checked against this same guitar's bridge measured by Mores (2021, open data): its lowest resonances have quality factors of 20 to 38 there, where the model's body, with its wood's loss alone, has 55 to 112. At the treble E string the model's body is about twice as heavy as measured in its two lowest resonances (599 and 231 g against about 370 and 110 g), and between resonances it takes two to four times less energy from the string than the real body does from 400 to 900 Hz. This is a main reason the upper partials ring too long. The model's resonance frequencies agree with the measurement within 4 percent, and its shell weighs about 800 g, plausible for a 1495 g guitar without its neck, so it is the shape of the low modes, with the back taking a large share of the motion, that puts too much mass at the strings. The air's two-way load on the body, the bridge as printed (4.5 mm wings and the saddle recess), and the neck and fingerboard are the physics still to add; none of them is tuned to this measurement
Radiation is the compact observation, not a boundary-element microphone with fluid loading
The stretched-string state (the working tension of a real nylon string is below the unstretched-mass value) is not modelled
